analysis.one_liner: Let states and the FCC cap cable TV rates and set service standards where cable faces no real competition.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 1991 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1984, Congress stripped states and cities of the power to regulate cable TV rates, betting that competition would hold prices down. Competition never came, and cable bills rose far faster than inflation: the cheapest cable service rose about 43% between 1986 and 1989, roughly triple the rate of inflation. This bill would let states, certified by the FCC, regulate cable rates again where no competitor exists, and would set federal standards for signal quality, customer service, and billing. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 59% of TV households that subscribed to cable at the time, most of whom had only one cable company to choose from. The bill would cap what a monopoly cable operator could charge, require honest billing and faster repair response, and give customers a way to resolve complaints. It would also help local broadcast stations by requiring cable systems to carry them, and help would-be competitors like satellite providers by barring cable-affiliated programmers from refusing to sell them programming.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cable subscribers with no provider choice

how_it_helps.text: Lets a state, once certified by the FCC, regulate all cable rates (including fees and deposits) in any cable system lacking 'effective competition,' which the bill defines so that a system serving most households in its area is presumed to be a monopoly [S3].

Sets federal customer service standards covering office hours, installation and repair response times, billing and refunds, disclosure of prices and tiers, and complaint procedures, while letting states and cities set stricter rules [S3].
Requires the FCC to set minimum technical standards for signal quality and to collect annual financial information from cable operators so rate decisions rest on real numbers [S3].

Bars cable-affiliated programming companies from unreasonably refusing to sell their channels to rival distributors or discriminating on price to block retail competition, and bars cable systems from demanding ownership stakes in programmers as a condition of carriage [S3].
Ties cable's compulsory license to broadcast programming under the Copyright Act to carrying local independent and public TV stations on the basic tier [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, whose monopoly rates and service practices would come under regulation for the first time since 1986, and programmers partly owned by cable companies, who would lose the ability to squeeze rival distributors. Compliance and rate-review costs would likely show up partly in subscriber bills, but the bill's premise is that regulated prices would be lower than unregulated monopoly prices.

drawbacks.text: Rate regulation of a capital-intensive network industry can discourage investment in plant and new services; the bill's own text acknowledges this tension by guaranteeing cable operators a 'reasonable profit' in rate determinations, but an honest supporter would admit price controls are a blunt tool that regulators can get wrong [S3].

The must-carry provision forces cable systems to devote channels to local broadcast stations, which reduces channel capacity available to other programmers and shifts carriage costs across all subscribers [S2].

The bill also caps court remedies against franchising authorities to injunctions and declarations, shielding local governments from damages suits arising from franchise decisions, a provision that protects government entities rather than consumers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households locked into a single cable provider, the upside is concrete: their bills rose about three times faster than inflation in the late 1980s, and this bill targets exactly that gap. The main costs fall on cable companies and their affiliated programmers, though heavy-handed rate regulation and mandatory carriage of local stations carry real risks of reduced investment and channel space. On balance this is a consumer-protection bill whose costs land mostly on a concentrated industry, with some design choices, like the franchising-authority liability shield, that serve governments rather than subscribers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Joseph Lieberman introduced the Cable Consumer Protection Act of 1991 on January 15, 1991 [S1].

The bill's findings state that under the 1984 Cable Act, states and franchising authorities were barred from directly reviewing rates in 97% of cable franchises, and that between 1986 and 1989 the cheapest cable service rose 43.1% and the most popular rose 39.4%, while the Consumer Price Index rose only about 12% [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote, and no cosponsors joined [S4].
The bill's own findings cite the FCC's conclusion that 'there currently is insufficient competition to provide a check on the quality of service offered by cable operators' [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators kept the unregulated monopoly rates they had enjoyed since 1986 for the remainder of the Congress, and cable subscribers kept paying prices rising roughly twice the rate of inflation.

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case in its findings that cable rates had risen far faster than inflation since deregulation [S3].

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee from January 1991 until the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Cable television industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed rate re-regulation after the 1984 Cable Act had freed them from state and local rate oversight; this bill targeted an industry that had just won deregulation and whose rates it would cap.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other senator cosponsored the bill, so there is no record of how either party would have lined up [S4].

industries.note: The bill would end the rate deregulation they had enjoyed since 1986, letting states and the FCC cap rates wherever fewer than 30% of households have a competing provider, and would impose federal customer service and signal quality standards. Their rates had risen about 40% in three years, so the bill's premise is that their monopoly pricing was costing subscribers real money [S3].

Programmers partly owned by cable companies could no longer refuse to sell channels to rival distributors like satellite services, nor charge rivals worse terms to protect cable's retail position [S3].

The must-carry provision requires cable systems to carry local independent and public stations as a condition of keeping their compulsory copyright license, which the bill argues is essential to the stations' survival [S3].

industries.industry: Satellite and other competing video distributors
industries.note: The nondiscrimination rules would make it harder for cable-affiliated programmers to withhold popular channels from satellite and other competitors, strengthening the alternatives the bill's effective-competition test depends on [S3].
